concepts.name: Government of India Act 1858: Structure and Significance
key_dimensions: How it formally abolished the East India Company and transferred power to the British Crown
Distinction between the Act of 1858 and the Charter Acts that preceded it — what changed and what continued
Why the Act is called a 'constitutional landmark' vs. merely an administrative reshuffle
UPSC trap: confusing the Act of 1858 with the Indian Councils Act of 1861 — both are post-1857 but serve different purposes

concepts.name: Secretary of State for India: Office, Powers, and Council
key_dimensions: Creation of the office of Secretary of State for India and his position in the British Cabinet
The Council of India — composition (15 members), functions, and advisory vs. binding nature of its advice
How the Secretary of State differed from the Board of Control under the Pitt's India Act 1784
UPSC trap: Secretary of State vs. Viceroy — who had ultimate authority, and in what domains did each operate

concepts.name: Abolition of the East India Company: Institutional Mechanics
key_dimensions: The precise legal mechanism by which the Company's authority was extinguished — what assets, armies, and liabilities were transferred
Fate of the Company's Court of Directors and Board of Control after 1858
Continuity vs. rupture: which Company-era laws, services, and structures were retained by the Crown
UPSC trap: the Company was not abolished immediately after the revolt began — the Act came into effect on November 1, 1858

concepts.name: Queen's Proclamation of 1858: Promises and Their Implications
key_dimensions: Key promises made — non-interference in religion, equal opportunity in public service, respect for treaties with Indian princes
The Proclamation as a quasi-constitutional document: its legal enforceability vs. political significance
Comparison with the actual policies that followed — how far promises were honoured (civil services, princely states)
UPSC trap: the Proclamation promised equal public service access, but the Indian Councils Act 1861 and the age barrier in ICS effectively negated this

concepts.name: Office of Viceroy: Creation, Powers, and Distinction from Governor-General
key_dimensions: Lord Canning as the first Viceroy — the title change from Governor-General and its symbolic significance
Difference in the constitutional position of Governor-General under Company rule vs. Viceroy under Crown rule
Dual accountability: to the Secretary of State and, indirectly, to the British Parliament
UPSC trap: Canning held both titles simultaneously for a transitional period — he was the last Governor-General AND first Viceroy

concepts.name: Reorganisation of the Indian Army after 1857
key_dimensions: The 'White Mutiny' of 1859 — European Company troops resisting transfer to Crown service, and how it was resolved
New ratio policy: increased proportion of European to Indian soldiers, especially in artillery
The 'divide and rule' principle in army recruitment — introduction of the 'martial races' theory
UPSC trap: the reorganisation was not uniform — different policies applied to Bengal Army (most implicated) vs. Bombay and Madras armies

concepts.name: Policy Toward Princely States: Doctrine of Lapse Abandoned
key_dimensions: Formal abandonment of Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse as part of the post-1857 conciliatory policy
The Queen's Proclamation promise to respect 'rights, dignity, and honour' of Indian princes
How the relationship shifted from annexation to 'paramountcy' — princes as subordinate allies rather than targets
UPSC trap: abandonment of the Doctrine of Lapse did not mean full sovereignty for princes — the doctrine of Paramountcy replaced it as a tool of control

concepts.name: Indian Councils Act 1861: Legislative and Executive Reforms
key_dimensions: Expansion of the Viceroy's Executive Council — addition of a fifth (law) member and the principle behind it
Introduction of non-official (Indian) members to legislative councils — symbolic inclusion vs. real power
Restoration of legislative powers to Bombay and Madras councils — significance of decentralisation
UPSC trap: the Act gave Indians nominal legislative representation but no executive power — often confused with meaningful constitutional reform

concepts.name: Financial Reorganisation and the India Office Finances
key_dimensions: How the enormous debt incurred suppressing the revolt was charged to Indian revenues — the 'drain' dimension
Creation of a separate India budget and the role of the Secretary of State's Council in financial oversight
The controversy over 'Home Charges' — what they included and how they became a nationalist grievance
UPSC trap: financial control nominally moved to Parliament via the Secretary of State, but Indians had no say — often presented as 'accountability'

concepts.name: Changes in Civil Services: ICS Entry and Racial Discrimination
key_dimensions: Queen's Proclamation promise of equal access to public service 'without distinction of race or creed'
Practical barriers retained — ICS examination held only in London until 1922, age limit lowered from 23 to 19 in 1876
Distinction between covenanted (ICS) and uncovenanted (subordinate) services and their racial composition
UPSC trap: the formal promise of equality in 1858 vs. the Aitchison Commission (1886) recommendations that further entrenched racial hierarchy in services

concepts.name: The 'Divide and Conquer' Policy: Religious and Communal Dimensions
key_dimensions: How the British interpreted the revolt as partly a Hindu-Muslim alliance and decided to forestall future unity
Differential policies toward Hindus and Muslims in the immediate aftermath — especially punitive measures against Muslims in Delhi
Long-term communal policy: patronising one community against the other depending on political expediency
UPSC trap: the shift in British attitude toward Muslims — from post-1857 suspicion to post-1870s favouritism — is a frequently tested policy reversal

concepts.name: Racialisation of British Policy and the 'Lessons of 1857'
key_dimensions: How 1857 entrenched racial distance — cantonments separated, social mixing discouraged, the 'white town/black town' divide institutionalised
The Arms Act 1878 and Vernacular Press Act 1878 as direct institutional consequences of the fear of another revolt
British historiography of 1857 as a 'mutiny' vs. Indian nationalist reinterpretation — and why this framing mattered for policy
UPSC trap: the Arms Act (1878) is often linked to Lord Lytton, not directly to 1857, but its ideological roots lie in the post-1857 racialisation of security policy

concepts.name: End of Mughal Sovereignty: Trial and Exile of Bahadur Shah Zafar
key_dimensions: The trial of Bahadur Shah Zafar — legal basis, charges, and the political message it sent about the end of Mughal legitimacy
Exile to Rangoon and the symbolic closure of the Mughal era as a legitimising force in Indian politics
How the British used the trial to delegitimise the revolt by portraying it as a dynastic conspiracy rather than a popular uprising
UPSC trap: Bahadur Shah was not executed — he died in exile in 1862 — a frequently confused fact

concepts.name: Parliamentary Oversight of Indian Governance post-1858
key_dimensions: Role of the British Parliament in Indian affairs — annual India budget presentation, question hour, and select committees
How parliamentary oversight was structurally limited — the Secretary of State could override Parliament on Indian matters
Comparison with Company-era oversight: the Board of Control vs. the new Secretary of State system — which was more accountable?
UPSC trap: Parliament had formal oversight but rarely exercised it effectively — Indian nationalists later used this gap to argue for direct Indian representation

concepts.name: Nationalist Reinterpretation of 1857 and Its Political Consequences
key_dimensions: V.D. Savarkar's 'The Indian War of Independence 1857' (1909) — first systematic nationalist reinterpretation and why it was banned
How the reinterpretation shifted from 'mutiny' (British view) to 'first war of independence' (nationalist view) — historiographical stakes
Use of 1857's memory in later nationalist mobilisation — the 1907 and 1957 commemorations
UPSC trap: Savarkar wrote the book in 1909 but it was published abroad — it was banned in India and Britain before it was formally published, a unique bibliographic fact

concepts.name: Economic Consequences: Drain of Wealth and War Debt
key_dimensions: The cost of suppressing the revolt (estimated £40 million+) charged to Indian revenues — the 'war indemnity' dimension
How the revolt accelerated British infrastructure investment (railways, telegraph) as a counter-insurgency tool — dual economic motive
Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain theory' and its connection to the financial settlement after 1858
UPSC trap: British infrastructure investment post-1857 is sometimes presented as benevolent development — Naoroji and later Romesh Chunder Dutt showed it was strategically self-serving

concepts.name: Transfer of Power Proclamation: November 1, 1858 — Date and Ceremony
key_dimensions: The Allahabad Durbar of November 1, 1858 — where and how the Proclamation was read, and its ceremonial-political significance
Lord Canning's role in both the suppression of the revolt and the proclamation of the new order — the same figure bridging both phases
Why Allahabad was chosen — its symbolic location at the confluence (Prayag) and its role as a centre of British power in North India
UPSC trap: the Proclamation was read at multiple locations across India simultaneously — it was not a single ceremony, a detail that underscores its administrative nature

concepts.name: Long-term Constitutional Legacy: 1858 as a Bridge to 1909, 1919, and 1935
key_dimensions: How the Government of India Act 1858 established the constitutional template that subsequent Acts modified rather than replaced
The 1858 Act's silence on Indian political representation — the void that Morley-Minto (1909) was later forced to address
Continuity of the Viceroy-Secretary of State dual authority structure through 1858 → 1919 → 1935
UPSC trap: each subsequent Government of India Act is an amendment to the 1858 framework, not a fresh start — understanding 1858 is prerequisite to understanding the entire constitutional evolution
